enhanced.fullText:
The Bayh-Dole Act of 1980, codified at 35 U.S.C. §§ 200-212, revolutionized federal technology transfer policy by allowing universities, small businesses, and nonprofit organizations to retain title to inventions developed with federal funding. This landmark legislation, implemented through 37 C.F.R. Part 401, fundamentally shifted from government ownership to institutional ownership of federally-funded innovations.

Under 35 U.S.C. § 202, universities must establish written patent policies and procedures for handling subject inventions. The Act requires disclosure of all potentially patentable inventions to federal funding agencies within two months of disclosure to institutional personnel responsible for patent matters (35 U.S.C. § 202(c)(1)). Universities must then elect title within two years and file patent applications within one year of election, or earlier if required by the funding agency.

The government retains certain march-in rights under 35 U.S.C. § 203, allowing agencies to require licensing to third parties if universities fail to achieve practical application or fail to satisfy health and safety needs. Universities must grant the government a nonexclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid-up license to practice the invention worldwide (35 U.S.C. § 202(c)(4)).

Preference for U.S. manufacturing is mandated under 35 U.S.C. § 204, requiring that products embodying subject inventions be substantially manufactured in the United States unless waived by the funding agency. Universities cannot assign rights without agency approval except to organizations with effective patent management capabilities.

Compliance obligations include maintaining invention disclosure systems, ensuring inventor agreements cover federal funding obligations, and submitting utilization reports biennially using iEdisonWeb system as required by 37 C.F.R. § 401.14(h). The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) oversees government-wide implementation.

Enforcement mechanisms include funding termination, requirement to assign title to the government, and potential False Claims Act liability for non-compliance. Recent updates include streamlined reporting requirements and enhanced march-in procedures clarification through Federal Register notices in 2021-2023.

Universities must establish technology transfer offices to manage patent prosecution, licensing activities, and revenue sharing with inventors. The Act's success is measured by its generation of over $1.9 trillion in economic impact since enactment, demonstrating its critical role in American innovation ecosystem.
enhanced.summary: Federal law enabling universities to retain patent rights for federally-funded inventions. Requires disclosure within 60 days, title election within 2 years, and biennial utilization reporting. Universities must grant government license and prefer U.S. manufacturing.
enhanced.requirements:
## Invention Management and Disclosure
- Establish written patent policies covering all federally-funded research projects
- Disclose subject inventions within 60 days to funding agencies via iEdisonWeb
- Maintain confidential invention disclosure processes with research personnel
- Execute agreements with employees covering invention disclosure obligations

## Title Election and Patent Filing
- Elect title to inventions within 2 years of disclosure to agency (or earlier if specified)
- File patent applications within 1 year of title election
- Provide agency with patent filing information and prosecution updates
- Obtain written approval before assigning patent rights to third parties

## Licensing and Manufacturing Requirements
- Grant nonexclusive government license for all subject inventions
- Ensure substantial U.S. manufacturing for licensed products (or obtain waiver)
- Implement preference for small business licensing arrangements
- Share licensing revenues appropriately with inventors per institutional policy

## Compliance Monitoring
- Submit biennial utilization reports through iEdisonWeb system
- Maintain records of invention disclosures, patent filings, and licensing activities
- Respond to agency requests for march-in proceedings information
enhanced.reportingRequirements: Biennial utilization reports due every two years via iEdisonWeb system detailing commercialization status, licensing revenue, and manufacturing locations. Annual invention summary reports to funding agencies. Event-triggered reporting for licensing agreements, patent issuance, and commercialization milestones within 60 days of occurrence.
